definition: In the 2020s, the rapid advancement of deep learning-based generative artificial intelligence models raised questions about the copyright status of AI-generated works, and about whether copyright infringement occurs when such are trained or used.
details: This includes text-to-image models such as Stable Diffusion and large language models such as GPT. Large language models are trained on all the data which can be scraped from the Internet, often utilizing copyrighted material. As of 2023, there were several pending U.S. lawsuits challenging the use of copyrighted data to train AI models, with defendants arguing that this falls under fair use.

explainer.lead: Artificial intelligence and copyright covers two connected questions: who, if anyone, owns material made with AI, and whether copyrighted works can lawfully be used to train AI systems. The answers affect artists, writers, software teams, and anyone publishing AI-assisted work.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a machine that makes a new picture after studying millions of existing pictures. People disagree about whether using those pictures for study was allowed, and whether the new picture belongs to the machine's user, its maker, or nobody. If a person carefully chooses and arranges the results, that person's creative contribution may matter.
tiers.practitioner: Teams using generative AI should distinguish training-data disputes from questions about protecting the resulting work. In US registration practice, applicants may need to disclose AI-generated material, while human selection, arrangement, editing, or other evident creative expression can support copyright in an AI-assisted work. Do not assume that a prompt alone guarantees protection or that a fair-use defense has settled training on copyrighted data.
tiers.paperLevel: The problem separates into protectability—whether originality and legally recognized authorship exist—and infringement—whether training or use of copyrighted material is unlawful, with fair use raised as a defense in US training litigation. US guidance treats machine-determined expressive elements as uncopyrightable, while evident human creative expression, including selection and arrangement, may be protected; the UK's Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 instead assigns authorship of computer-generated works to the person undertaking the arrangements necessary for their creation. A central limit is that outputs produced without human intervention are treated differently from works with demonstrable human authorship, and the training disputes described remained pending as of 2023.

explainer.example: Jason Matthew Allen created Théâtre D'opéra Spatial using Midjourney and an upscaling tool. The US Copyright Office found more than a de minimis amount of AI-generated content and said it had to be disclaimed; because Allen would not do so, the work could not be registered as submitted.

usedIn.name: US copyright registration
usedIn.detail: The Copyright Office assesses human authorship and requests disclosure of more than a de minimis amount of AI-generated content.

explainer.intuition: Copyright law asks both how an AI system learned and how much recognizable human creativity went into a particular result. A model's output is not automatically protected merely because someone requested it, and using an existing work as training data is not automatically lawful merely because a model produced something new.
howItWorks: Identify the material used in training and whether it includes copyrighted works.
For training disputes, consider the alleged infringement and defenses such as fair use in the United States.
For an output, separate machine-generated expression from human prompts, edits, selection, arrangement, and coordination.
Apply the relevant jurisdiction's authorship rule when deciding whether any part can be registered or protected.
When seeking US registration, disclose AI-generated material as required rather than claiming it as human-authored work.
explainer.whyItMatters: These rules shape whether creators can protect AI-assisted work and whether developers face liability for their training practices. They also determine what applicants must disclose and what evidence of human creativity may support registration.
misconceptions: Using AI does not always make an entire work uncopyrightable; evident human creative expression may still be protected in the United States.
A fair-use defense is not a general ruling that all AI training on copyrighted material is lawful.
Jurisdictions differ: the United Kingdom has a specific statutory authorship rule for computer-generated works.
Copyright in AI outputs and patent inventorship are separate issues, although both have raised human-authorship or natural-person requirements.
